question: How can a finale keep surprising with three small ideas?
intro: A dancing tune opens in the strings alone, and the whole finale is built from a few small ideas: the tune’s upbeat, a run of sixteenth notes and its closing turn. Watch how Haydn reorders them, shortens the return and ends quietly before a last burst.

cues.title: Strings first, then a flute
cues.text: The finale opens piano with the strings alone: a dancing, periodic theme. On its repeat a flute joins, a contrasting string phrase follows, and the theme returns with flute and bassoon before the first tutti.
cues.evidence: German Wikipedia’s analysis of the finale (https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)) and the score (IMSLP #546546, printed pp. 35–36) give the strings-only first statement, the flute on the repeat and flute and bassoon with the theme before the tutti. The report’s opening window is −35.1 dB; no entry is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first full forte
cues.text: At about 0:30 the whole orchestra comes in at once, the level jumping by about nine decibels. The key estimate turns to D major, the dominant: Haydn leaves the opening G major within half a minute.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −17.5 dB at 0:25 to −8.8 dB at 0:30, with the key estimate moving to D major soon after and staying there through 1:15; a boundary at 0:34 (0.41). The score’s first full-orchestra forte is in these bars; none is aligned.

cues.title: A London first night
cues.text: The symphony was first played at the Hanover Square Rooms in London on 23 March 1792, with Haydn at the fortepiano. A critic of Woodfall’s Register called the new overture “of very extraordinary merit”.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 94 article gives the premiere date and venue, Haydn at the fortepiano, and the Woodfall’s Register review: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._94_(Haydn).

cues.title: A second tune over a repeated D
cues.text: Around 0:55 a new tune appears, again piano and in the strings, while the bass keeps repeating D. It is the music that will reappear later in G. Listen to it so you recognise it when it returns a fourth higher.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 0:54 (0.32) and 0:58 (0.38) with the key estimate D major at 0:55–1:15; a recurrence analysis matches 56.5–68.5 s with 161.0–173.0 s at five semitones upward (D to G; similarity 0.96). The repeated D in the bass and the string scoring are German Wikipedia’s description.

cues.title: Strokes on C, and the theme again
cues.text: At about 1:18 the exposition ends and the development begins with repeated quarter-note strokes on C. They act as a dominant seventh to the first theme in G major, so that for a moment it sounds as if the exposition were beginning again.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 1:18 (novelty 0.38); the level is −23.9 dB at 1:20 and −13.0 dB at 1:25, with the key estimate G major at 1:20. The strokes on C and the G-major theme are German Wikipedia’s description of the development (from bar 99 or 103); no bar is aligned.

cues.title: The harmony turns restless
cues.text: Between about 1:35 and 1:50 the development is at its most turbulent. The strongest boundary of the movement (1:42) and its loudest window (1:45) fall here, with 1:40 also among the five loudest and a bass the report reads on F♯.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:42 (novelty 1.00); levels are −8.6 dB at 1:40 and −7.4 dB at 1:45, the loudest window of the file; 1:40 is fifth loudest. The bass reading F♯ is an audio estimate, not a score fact. German Wikipedia describes rapid harmonic change from bar 121; the bars are not aligned.

cues.title: The theme in G minor
cues.text: After a very quiet window at 1:50 the first theme returns forte, in G minor, at about 1:54. It starts a modulating stretch through flat keys that the report reads as B♭ in the bass at 2:00 and 2:05.
cues.evidence: Level falls to −31.4 dB at 1:50 (a quietest window); boundaries at 1:54 (0.75) and 1:58 (0.74); the key estimate reads G minor at 2:00–2:05 (r 0.69, 0.76) with B♭ in the bass, then D major at 2:10–2:20 (r 0.63–0.71). The G-minor forte statement and the modulation through E♭, F and B♭ major are German Wikipedia’s description (from bar 146); no bar is aligned.

cues.title: A shortened return
cues.text: At about 2:21 the recapitulation begins in G major, and it is shortened: the repeats of the first theme are left out, so the return opens directly with the theme’s contrasting B part. The recording matches the exposition’s opening bars closely.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 7.5–21.5 s with 141.0–155.0 s (offset 133.5 s, no transposition, similarity 0.97); the key estimate reads D major at 2:15 and G major from 2:25. The shortened return, which comes straight to the B part, is German Wikipedia’s description (bar 182; bar 145 in the Philharmonia edition); the matched stretch is an approximate window, and the first bar is not aligned.

cues.title: The second tune, now in G
cues.text: By about 2:41 the second tune is back, five semitones above where it sounded in the exposition. The harmony has settled on the home key.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches the exposition’s 56.5–68.5 s with 161.0–173.0 s transposed up five semitones; the local key reads G major at 2:25–3:20 (r 0.64–0.87). The first bar of the return is not aligned.

cues.title: A quiet coda, a roll, a detour
cues.text: The coda begins quietly at about 2:55, with the first idea in piano. A timpani roll then turns loud one bar before the rest of the orchestra, a small echo of the Andante’s surprise, and the music swerves to E♭ major with the first theme in forte.
cues.evidence: Level is −23.9 dB at 2:55 with low brightness, then −16.4 dB at 3:00 and −14.5 dB at 3:05; boundaries at 2:50 (0.35), 3:02 (0.33) and 3:08 (0.33). The quiet start, the timpani roll, its early forte and the turn to E♭ major are German Wikipedia’s description (coda from bar 222); the E♭ passage is not separately identified in the report.

cues.title: Fortissimo chords at the end
cues.text: The movement ends with chords in fortissimo. The windows at 3:10, 3:15 and 3:20 are among the loudest of the file, and the sound drops away by 3:25.
cues.evidence: Levels are −7.6, −7.6 and −7.7 dB at 3:10, 3:15 and 3:20, with 1:45 (−7.4 dB) the loudest window of the file; −29.4 dB at 3:25 and −62.8 dB at 3:30, the file’s end. The fortissimo chord ending is German Wikipedia’s description.

transitions.title: Strokes on C, the exposition seems to restart
transitions.from: Exposition · G major to D major
transitions.to: Development · strokes on C, the theme in G, a turn to G minor
transitions.how: The exposition ends with forte strokes on D and runs straight on, without a repeat. The development opens with repeated quarter-note strokes on C, which act as a dominant seventh to the first theme in G major, so that the theme seems to start the exposition again. Then, from about bar 112, the closing turn of the theme moves to the bass and the harmony changes sharply.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 1:18 (0.38); the level is −23.9 dB at 1:20 and −13.0 dB at 1:25. The three forte strokes on D, the strokes on C and the G-major theme are German Wikipedia’s description (bars 99–112); no bar is aligned.

transitions.title: Back through D to a shortened return
transitions.from: Development · strokes on C, the theme in G, a turn to G minor
transitions.how: After the forte statement in G minor the music modulates through E♭, F and B♭ major, returns to D major, the dominant, and runs out in sixteenth notes in the first violin. The recapitulation then begins in G major. It is a shortened version of the exposition: the repeats of the first theme are omitted, so it opens directly with the theme’s B part, and the stretch between the two main themes is cut.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 7.5–21.5 s with 141.0–155.0 s; the key estimate reads B♭ in the bass at 2:00–2:05, D major at 2:10–2:20 and G major from 2:25; boundaries at 2:10 (0.37), 2:14 (0.35) and 2:20 (0.40). The modulation, the return to D and the shortened reprise are German Wikipedia’s description (bars 160–195); no bar is aligned.

transitions.title: A hush, a roll, and E♭
transitions.to: Coda · quiet, a timpani roll, an E♭ detour
transitions.how: The second theme in G is followed immediately by the coda. The first idea sounds piano, then a timpani roll turns forte a bar before the other instruments and the music swerves to E♭ major with the first theme in forte, a sideways step after the quiet. The movement ends with chords in fortissimo, with the closing turn of the theme set in between.
transitions.evidence: Level is −18.6 dB at 2:50 and −23.9 dB at 2:55 with low brightness, then −16.4 dB at 3:00 and −7.6 dB at 3:10; boundaries at 2:50 (0.35), 3:02 (0.33) and 3:08 (0.33). The coda’s quiet start, the timpani roll with its early forte, the E♭ turn and the closing chords are German Wikipedia’s description (bars 222–268); no bar is aligned.

timeline.note: Strings alone for the first statement of the theme.
A flute joins the repeat of the theme, and flute and bassoon join its return, before the tutti.
The coda begins quietly; a timpani roll then turns forte ahead of the rest of the orchestra, and the full orchestra closes the movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Young lists CVE-48988 with the recording date 24 April 1929, DAHR lists it among the Boston Symphony Orchestra and Koussevitzky recordings of Symphony No. 94 made that day, and the Bolig discography assigns the finale (“Allegro di molto”) to that matrix. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CVE-48988, take 2 or take 3: the finale; the take on this transfer is not identified
fields.note: Young lists both take 2 and take 3 of CVE-48988 as issued (three takes made), and Bolig names take 3. Which take the Bob Varney transfer reproduces is not established by any source consulted, so only the matrix is asserted. The DAHR matrix page could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
